doc.title: A.B. Spellman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 19, 2022

title: Whether great art needs misery
summary: Responding to Benny Powell, he rejects the myth that artists must be miserable.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Looking back: no regrets, what it all meant

blocks.x: I had the good fortune to interview the trombone player Benny Powell. And he said in his opinion no great art ever came from happiness — that there had to be adversity for, he said “great art to be formed.” And I wonder how you feel about that?

I don’t think that’s true. That’s one of the myths about art is that you’ve got to be miserable and alienated. That isn’t true at all. I’ve been happy most of my life, not to name myself a great artist but I don’t find that I made better work when I was depressed and miserable than I did when I was happy. I don’t think that’s true of other artists as well. I feel like Cecil Taylor, he wasn’t a miserable person. He was basically in a good mood every time I saw him, most times that I saw him at any rate. Coltrane was a quiet guy but I don’t look on his as being a sad and miserable person. So no, I think that you know that’s one of the myths that goes along with things like the blues you know what I mean? But even the blues is not a miserable form. I mean most blues songs are quite up, quite joyful.
